Have my recipe for chocolate rum cake:

For the cake: (I use a bundt pan) 1 box (18.25 oz) chocolate cake mix (I use Pillsbury Devil's Food) 1 box (3.9 oz) instant chocolate pudding 4 eggs 1/2 cup water 1/2 cup veggie oil 1/2 cup gold rum (I use Flor de Cana) Chopped walnuts, if you're into that.

For the pour-over: 1/2 cup (or 1 stick) butter 1 cup dark brown sugar 1/4 cup gold rum 1/4 cup water

Preheat to 325*F. Mix and beat the cake ingredients all together for two minutes (the color of the batter will lighten; it will also become very thick). Pour that viscous deliciousness into a greased pan and bake it until a toothpick comes out clean. That's maybe 45-60 minutes depending on your oven and how warm it is in your kitchen anyway.

While it's in the oven, make the pour-over stuff! Melt butter in a small saucepan. Add the wet ingredients and mix in the dark brown sugar. Set heat to medium. Do not leave the stove unattended, but stir periodically, and stir frequently once it starts to bubble. After it bubbles for a minute or two (and seriously, don't walk away, you will have a MESS), take it off the heat and set it aside, stirring until you're ready to pour it over the cake.

When your cake's done, take a chopstick (or knife, I guess!) and poke holes in it all around the cake. I usually do three circular rows, spaced about an inch apart side-to-side. Pour the rum syrup into the holes in the cake. Cover with aluminum foil and just let it sit. After 8 hours, or the next day, flip it over for an hour or so. Tastes best if at least a day or two old. :)

Chicken Fajita Burrito

Ingredients

  • 1.5 pounds of chicken breast
  • 1 cup dry rice
  • 2 cups shredded cheese (I like colby jack, but choose your favorite)
  • can of refried beans (you can cut the calories by using regular beans)
  • 8 burrito tortillas
  • 0.5 cup salsa
  • fajita seasoning

Directions

  1. Coat chicken in fajita seasoning. Set aside for a few hours.
  2. Cook rice to directions
  3. Cook chicken, shred to preference.
  4. In a bowl, combine rice, beans, salsa, chicken, and cheese.
  5. Portion filling evenly into tortillas and wrap it up.

These keep nicely in the fridge. You can reheat them 300F for 30 minutes.

Nutrition per burrito

  • 569 calories
  • 14.7 grams of fat
  • 62.5 grams of carbohydrates
  • 36.6 grams of protein

In short: empathy.

Empathy is not sympathy. It doesn't mean agreeing with someone; it just means trying to understand their situation, their reasoning, their perspective. Nobody can see you better than those who oppose you, because they watch you like a hawk. Therefore, walking in their shoes gives you the best view of yourself you'll ever have. And we need to be self-aware.

I've been reading a lot about conflict resolution. (I highly recommend Dr. George J. Thompson's "Verbal Judo" to everyone)

I firmly believe the following because I've found it to work personally:

  • Everybody wants to be treated with dignity and respect.
  • Everybody would rather be asked than told.
  • Everybody would prefer to know WHY they're being asked or told
  • Everybody likes having a second chance.

You may not feel like someone deserves dignity or respect; Hell, you might even be right.

But the reason you treat someone with dignity and respect isn't because they deserve it, but because YOU HAVE IT.

Professionalism sets the tone. Furthermore, it breaks their oppositional narrative. They expect hostility. They expect to be screamed at and cursed. They revel in it, because to them it means victory. If you maintain sincere professionalism, it derails everything. They'll attempt to escalate again and again, but if you empathize, show them patience, conduct yourself with integrity, and make a due diligence effort of respect, they will have no idea what to do. Sometimes, they get so desperate they even try it themselves.

Remember these. Integrity, Respect, Empathy, Patience, Affability, Cooperation. These are the Virtues of Professionalism.
I hope each of you will consider taking these virtues to heart. I know none of us are saints. We all have our dark vices. We all need to blow off steam. Don't count the failures; count the successes. Every interaction is an opportunity to hone your skill. Attempt to apply these in every day life, and I expect you'll be amazed with the results.

Remember also that this is a personal commitment and that no one else is 'required' to live up to it. It will affect them, but it won't necessarily be perfectly reflected within them. If you do this, though, you'll set an example. By doing the right thing, you become a leader. And if cooperative bonds form and build a community, no moderator or administrator will be able to stop it.

Good luck. But you might not need it.
